John Williams (missionary)
JON WIL-yumz
proper noun
John from the Hebrew Yōhānān, “the LORD is gracious”; Williams a common Welsh-English surname; he was hailed as “the Apostle of the South Seas.”

Biblical Definition

John Williams (1796–1839) was a missionary of the London Missionary Society to the South Sea Islands, hailed as “the Apostle of the South Seas” and at last martyred upon the shore of Erromango. Apprenticed as a youth to an ironmonger and skilled with his hands, he was converted in his teens and sailed with his wife to the Society Islands, where the gospel had already begun to break the long night of idolatry and human sacrifice. Restless to reach the islands yet untouched, he would not be confined to a single station; he built a ship with his own hands, the Messenger of Peace, and carried the gospel across vast reaches of the Pacific, raising up native teachers and planting churches on Rarotonga, Samoa, and beyond. Whole peoples turned from their idols to serve the living God, burning their gods and building houses of worship. His method of sending out converted islanders as evangelists multiplied the work far beyond what any band of Europeans could do. Returning from England with renewed zeal, he landed at Erromango in the New Hebrides, where the people, embittered by earlier outrages of traders, fell upon him and slew him. He poured out his blood as a seed of the church (Rev 2:10), and his death stirred a generation to take up the cause he had loved. He stands among the noblest laborers of the Great Commission.

Webster 1828 Definition

A London Missionary Society missionary to the South Sea Islands, called the Apostle of the South Seas, martyred at Erromango.

expand to see more

JOHN WILLIAMS, an English missionary (1796–1839) of the London Missionary Society to the islands of the South Pacific.

He built his own ship, the Messenger of Peace, to carry the gospel from island to island.

He planted churches on Rarotonga, Samoa, and many isles, and saw whole peoples forsake their idols.

He raised up converted islanders as native evangelists, multiplying the work across the Pacific.

He was martyred at Erromango in the New Hebrides in 1839 (Rev 2:10).

Key Scripture

Rev 2:10 — "Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried; and ye shall have tribulation ten days: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life."

1Th 1:9 — "For they themselves shew of us what manner of entering in we had unto you, and how ye turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God;"

Isa 42:4 — "He shall not fail nor be discouraged, till he have set judgment in the earth: and the isles shall wait for his law."

Rom 10:15 — "And how shall they preach, except they be sent? as it is written, How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, and bring glad tidings of good things!"

Modern Corruption

Williams’ island mission is recast by anti-missions revisionism as the destroyer of native culture, ignoring the cannibalism and idolatry from which the gospel freed the islands.

expand to see more

The revisionist account mourns the “lost” island cultures and indicts missionaries like Williams for erasing them. It passes over in silence what those cultures were: societies bound by idolatry, infant sacrifice, perpetual tribal slaughter, and in places cannibalism. The islanders who turned to God from idols (1Th 1:9) did not exchange freedom for bondage; they were delivered from death to life. To lament the passing of human sacrifice as the death of a culture is to prize custom above conscience, and to forget that the very compassion the critics invoke was carried to those shores by the gospel of peace.

The lesson to recover is that the gospel is glad tidings to the nations, not the imposition of one tribe upon another, and that the isles waited for His law (Isa 42:4). Williams did not conquer but built a ship to bring peace; he did not dominate but raised native teachers to carry the word in their own tongue. His blood at Erromango was the seed of the church, and the same Pacific that took his life soon resounded with the praise of God among peoples who had once known only fear. A faithful reckoning honors the martyr and exposes the revision as ingratitude.

Hebrew Roots

“The LORD is gracious” was his name, and the grace of God was his message to the waiting isles.

expand to see more

John — Hebrew Yōhānān, “the LORD is gracious.”

Williams — a Welsh-English surname; the man who bore it was apprenticed to ironwork before the gospel.

His ship he named the Messenger of Peace, after the gospel of peace (Rom 10:15).

“Apostle” from the Greek apostolos, “one sent forth,” aptly named his roving labor.

“Erromango” named the island shore where he sealed his witness with his blood.

Usage

"John Williams built the Messenger of Peace and carried the gospel across a thousand miles of ocean."

"Whole island peoples burned their idols when John Williams preached the living God among them."

"On the beach of Erromango John Williams laid down his life for the gospel he had brought to the isles."
